The Black-Powder Wars, 1618–1877

Nine battles from Gustavus Adolphus at Lützen in 1632 to the Wagon Box Fight in 1867: the Thirty Years' War, the American Revolution, the Peninsula and the War of 1812, the storming of the Great Redan before Sevastopol, the first battle of the American Civil War, and two fights on the Bozeman Trail against the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho. Every rule is in the Rules; this book holds the armies' figures for five eras, the wound tables their battles roll on, the battlefields, and a British company at Albuera followed through the morning of the lancers.

The battlefields: Lützen 1632, Cowpens 1781, Albuera 1811, Badajoz 1812, Lundy's Lane 1814, The Great Redan, 18 June 1855, The Great Redan, 8 September 1855, First Bull Run 1861, The Fetterman Fight 1866, The Wagon Box Fight 1867.

The period's fighting

The battles in this book run from 1632 to 1867, and its armies from 1618 to 1877. In those years gunpowder decided most fights. But most of what armies did was still marching, foraging, digging and falling sick, not battle.

Armies

In the Thirty Years' War most soldiers were hired men, serving in regiments under their colonels. Albrecht von Wallenstein raised the Emperor's army in the 1620s and, Peter Singer writes, became the richest man in Europe by it. Peter Wilson argues that credit, more than plunder, held the system together: princes and generals came to owe great sums to their colonels and men, which made armies hard to pay off and the war hard to end.

Sweden was different. Under Gustavus Adolphus's law of 1619 the parish priest listed every boy who reached 15. When the Riksdag voted a levy, the men were taken in groups of ten and one of each ten was chosen. These conscripts filled the infantry; the horse and the guns were mostly volunteers. They did not last. Lars Ericson counts the Swedish share of the king's army at about 85% in 1621, a little over half when it landed in Germany in 1630, and only 10 to 15% at Lützen. The rest were Germans, Scots and other hired men. Disease, cold and hunger killed far more of the conscripts than battle did.

By the American Revolution Britain kept a standing army, raised by voluntary enlistment. Recruiting parties with a drum worked the fairs and inns, and the bounty was the lure; in 1812 a man who signed on for life was promised nearly £24. Many were driven to it by poverty. The Continental Army first enlisted men for a year, as colonial troops had served. From late 1776 Congress set each state a quota of regiments and asked for men for three years or the war. Beside them served the states' militia, called out for a campaign, as at Cowpens.

Revolutionary France found another way. The levée en masse of 23 August 1793 called on the whole nation, and Caiani puts the army it raised at about 600,000. From 1798 France called a class of young men every year: conscription, which fed Napoleon's armies. The Russian army of the Crimea was drawn from serfs and other poll-tax payers, chosen by lot in their villages. In 1825 a line soldier served 25 years; the term was cut to 20 in 1834 and to 12 in 1855.

The American Civil War began with volunteers raised by the states. They came forward so fast in 1861 that some were turned away. The Confederacy passed a draft in April 1862 and the Union in 1863; both let a drafted man send a substitute, and the Union also let him pay $300. In the North the bounties were the lure: by the autumn of 1864 federal, state and town money together could come to $1,200 or more.

The Plains nations had no army. The men's societies gave the camp its order. Among the Cheyenne the societies (the Kit Foxes, the Elk Horn Scrapers, the Dog Men and others) took turns keeping discipline, policing the buffalo hunt and leading in war. The Dog Men became a band of their own and were the "Dog Soldiers" of the 1860s. Among the Lakota the council named akicita, marshals, who kept the camp and the hunt in order and could punish anyone who broke ranks. Honour came from counting coup: striking or touching an enemy and coming away unhurt counted for more than killing him.

Arms

In 1632 a musketeer fired a matchlock, its powder lit by a smouldering cord. The flintlock that replaced it fired about twice as fast and misfired less. Pikemen guarded the musketeers against horse. A Swedish company had about 4 muskets to 3 pikes, and as the century went on the musket gained. Between 1699 and 1708 the Imperial, French, English and Dutch armies gave up the pike, and the musketeer carried a bayonet instead.

The flintlock musket of the 18th century, Britain's "Brown Bess" or the French Charleville, fired a lead ball about 0.7 inch across. A trained man loaded and fired about 3 times a minute. The ball fitted loosely, so the musket was quick to load and inaccurate: a man could be hit at about 100 yards, and beyond that it was luck. Hence the volley. The rifle, grooved inside, was far more accurate but slower to load, and the American long rifle took no bayonet. Riflemen fought as skirmishers ahead of the line.

The percussion cap then replaced the flint and pan, and misfired much less in the wet. About 1849 Claude-Étienne Minié and others made the Minié ball: a conical bullet of soft lead, small enough to drop down a rifled barrel, whose base spread when fired to grip the grooves. Every infantryman could now carry a rifle that loaded as fast as a musket. The British and French had rifle-muskets in the Crimea; most Russian infantry still had smoothbores. In the Civil War the .58 Springfield and the Enfield were the common arms, accurate to about 500 yards.

Breech-loaders, loaded at the rear, came next. The Sharps fired perhaps 8 to 10 times a minute, and the Spencer, with a 7-round magazine, more. By 1867 the Army's infantry on the Bozeman Trail had breech-loading Springfields. The men at Fetterman's fight the year before had had muzzle-loaders, apart from the cavalry's carbines and two civilians' repeating rifles.

On the Plains most warriors fought with the bow, the lance, the club and the shield. Some had guns, traded or taken; after the Fetterman fight they had the dead soldiers' too.

The guns fired three kinds of round. Round shot, a solid iron ball, was mainly for battering walls and works, though it struck men too. Shell and spherical case were hollow and burst over the enemy on a fuse. Canister, a tin full of iron balls, turned a gun into a great shotgun out to about 400 yards.

Battles

Muskets that could not aim had to be fired together. So infantry fought in line, three ranks deep in most armies and two in the British, to bring every musket to bear. The line was slow and hard to keep. To march, to cross broken ground or to attack, battalions formed column, which moved faster and held nervous men together, then deployed into line to fire. Light infantry and riflemen skirmished in open order ahead of both.

Every shot made smoke, and with the dust of the fighting it could hide the field. At Raymond in 1863, Warren Grabau writes, smoke and dust cut the view to a few yards, and regiments came out of the woods where no one expected them. No one saw the whole of a battle, which is one reason the accounts of every field in this book disagree.

Horsemen still charged. Against them infantry formed a square, four ranks deep, the front two with bayonets out to keep off the horses and the rear two firing. The British squares at Waterloo are remembered for holding.

The rifle-musket changed less than men expected. It gave the defender more range and the attacker more ground to cross under fire, and the advantage moved to the defence. From the Crimea on, armies dug. The allies broke ground before Sevastopol in October 1854 and were still in their trenches when the last assault went in on 8 September 1855. The Union and Confederate armies faced each other in trenches at Petersburg for nine and a half months in 1864-65.

Wounds and surgeons

A soft lead ball did not pass cleanly through a man. It flattened and turned, shattered the bone it struck, and carried in pieces of cloth. The Civil War surgeons described the bullets they drew out as bent into "all imaginable forms". A ball through a limb bone often meant the limb had to come off. Amputation was the commonest operation of the Civil War: three of every four, one account says. Done quickly, it stopped the damage and saved many men. Those who kept a shattered limb often died of gangrene.

Until 1846 every operation was done on a man awake. On 16 October 1846, at the Massachusetts General Hospital, William Morton put Gilbert Abbott to sleep with ether while John Collins Warren operated on him. On 4 November 1847 James Young Simpson in Edinburgh found the effect of chloroform, and it soon replaced ether. Crimean and Civil War surgeons used both.

What no one understood was infection, and disease killed more than battle. Of about 21,000 British soldiers who died in the Crimean War, about 16,300 died of disease. Florence Nightingale reached the base hospital at Scutari, across from Constantinople, on 3 November 1854. The building sat on a broken sewer and had no fresh air; by February 1855 the death rate there had reached 42%. A man had a better chance in the hospitals at the front. The death rate fell only after a sanitary commission repaired the drains and the ventilation. In the Civil War about two-thirds of the roughly 620,000 dead died of disease. The US Sanitary Commission, founded in 1861, organised relief for the Union's sick and wounded, and Jonathan Letterman gave the Army of the Potomac an organised ambulance service.

Captain Molly

On 16 November 1776 British and Hessian troops stormed Fort Washington, on Manhattan. John Corbin, a Pennsylvania artilleryman, was killed at his gun. His wife Margaret had followed the regiment to cook, wash and nurse, and was beside him. She took over the gun and kept it firing until grapeshot struck her in the shoulder and chest. She probably never had the use of that arm again. On 6 July 1779 Congress gave her half a soldier's pay for life and a suit of clothes: the first pension the United States gave a woman for military service. She was known as "Captain Molly". She is not "Molly Pitcher", who is a composite legend drawn from several women; Mary Hays at Monmouth in 1778 is the other woman most often named.

Where the Girl Saved Her Brother

On 17 June 1876 Lakota and Cheyenne warriors met General Crook's column on Rosebud Creek, in Montana. During the fighting the soldiers shot the horse of Comes in Sight, a Cheyenne, and he fell. His sister, Buffalo Calf Road Woman, rode into the fighting, and with him clinging to her horse she carried him out under fire. A Cheyenne artist drew the ride in a ledger book now in the Smithsonian. The Cheyenne call the fight "Where the Girl Saved Her Brother". Eight days later she was at the Little Bighorn. She died of diphtheria in 1879, after her family had been taken prisoner to Fort Keogh.

The doctress

Mary Seacole, a Jamaican who had nursed cholera and yellow fever in the Caribbean and Panama, was in London when the war with Russia began. The War Office would not send her, and Florence Nightingale's party would not take her. She paid her own way. In 1855, with Thomas Day, she opened the "British Hotel" near Balaklava, a store, canteen and place to rest, and sold supplies and medicines to the army. She went up to the front to tend the wounded. When the army left in 1856 she came home with unsold stock and debts and was made bankrupt. Her book, Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands, came out in 1857.

Sieges and raids

Much of the war in these years was siege work. In the Thirty Years' War a town that would not yield could be stormed and sacked. When Tilly's army took Magdeburg on 20 May 1631, the town burned in a day; perhaps two-thirds of its 30,000 people were killed or died afterwards of hunger and exposure. Armies lived off the land. Jacques Callot's etchings of 1633, The Miseries of War, show soldiers looting farms and burning villages. Sevastopol and Petersburg were sieges of trench, battery and sap that lasted most of a year.

On the Plains, war was mostly raiding: for horses and honours against enemy nations such as the Crow and the Shoshone, and from 1866 against the wagon trains, wood trains and herds of the forts on the Bozeman Trail.

For the GM

Expect a black-powder fight to be decided at close range. The muskets of 1632 to 1815 hit little beyond 100 yards, and the volley and the charge settle it; the rifle-musket reaches farther but fights by the same rules. Guns matter most when the enemy comes close or comes deep: canister for the first, round shot through a column for the second. Men behind works are hard to shift, and the attacker must close and charge. Breech-loaders are different: against the Springfields at the Wagon Box, and the carbines and repeaters at the Fetterman fight, every serious wound puts a man down. After the fight, there are no antibiotics. Wound fever and the camp's sickness will kill more than the battle did, and a clean camp and a good surgeon are the only help.

What is switched on

The Black-powder guns module: batteries, misfires in the wet, and storming works with the bayonet. From the Modern fire module, only the rule that modern fire puts men down, and only for the breech-loaders: the soldiers' Springfields at the Wagon Box, and the carbines of Fetterman's cavalry and the civilians' repeating rifles. Muskets and rifle-muskets fight as the core rules say. Wounds heal and fester as the Rules' Recovery says, with no antibiotics.

Akicita (camp police) Command 50 unpaid 90-180 days village warrior with bow and shield, leader of war parties 10%

Trouble at work

Thirty Years' War (1618-1648)

d10 Trouble
1 Pay in arrears: no coin this term, only the paymaster's note.
2 The provost asks questions: prove you are not a deserter.
3 Peasants ambush the party: roll a wound.
4 Camp fever or plague: the term is lost to sickness.
5 Taken by the enemy and pressed into their regiment.
6 Robbed by comrades: half the term's take is gone.
7 A wife or comrade is taken by the enemy: ransom or rescue.
8 Debased coin: the pay is worth half.
9 An officer takes the booty as his share.
10 To be hanged as an example, unless someone speaks for him.

Horse and musket (1775-1815)

d10 Trouble
1 A press gang or crimp seizes him: argue or fight.
2 Taken up by the excise or a constable: fine, gaol or transportation.
3 Paid in bad paper or a ticket, worth 60% at best.
4 Fever or flux: the term is lost.
5 Robbed on the road or by a crimp.
6 A mob turns on him: roll a wound.
7 The employer goes bankrupt or flees, owing him.
8 A recruiting sergeant gets him drunk, and he wakes up enlisted.
9 Taken at sea: a prison hulk or Dartmoor.
10 An old crime comes to light: the assizes or a court-martial.

Crimean War (1854-1856)

d10 Trouble
1 Cholera: the term is lost, and a recovery check.
2 Pay stopped: a clerk has lost his name, and he must argue it back.
3 A shell or a stray shot falls on the works.
4 Theft: his kit or his earnings are gone.
5 A drunken brawl with navvies or Zouaves.
6 Accused of selling army stores.
7 Recalled to his regiment at once.
8 Frostbite or exposure on the col.
9 A Cossack patrol near the outposts.
10 An officer wants him as a servant, unpaid.

Civil War and frontier (1861-1876)

d10 Trouble
1 Guerrillas raid the train or the store.
2 The provost guard asks for his papers.
3 Fever or dysentery.
4 The employer skips town owing wages.
5 A stampede or a wagon wreck.
6 Swindled at cards.
7 Mistaken for a deserter.
8 A war party on the trail.
9 A brawl with soldiers.
10 Conscripted on the spot.

Plains nations (1860-1877)

d10 Trouble
1 An enemy war party finds the trail.
2 An army column or patrol.
3 A fall or a goring on the hunt.
4 The trader cheats, or brings whiskey.
5 A blizzard: horses lost.
6 The akicita punish a broken rule.
7 Smallpox or measles in camp.
8 Agency rations are held back.
9 A quarrel over horses or a woman.
10 A rival claims his coup.

What each skill is for

Thirty Years' War (1618-1648)

Skill Use Usually Against Success Failure Fumble
Persuade Haggle: Beat down a price. Ordinary the seller (Persuade) A tenth off (a quarter on a critical). The list price. No sale today.
Persuade Find a billet: Talk a village or a householder into a bed and a meal. Ordinary the householder or headman (Presence) Fed and bedded tonight: no keep to pay. He pays his keep, or sleeps rough. The village turns against the party: trouble.
Persuade Talk past a guard: Get by a sentry, a gate or the provost without the right papers. Hard the sentry or provost (Wits) Through. Turned back. Held as a deserter or a spy.
Persuade Question a prisoner: Get a prisoner or a local to talk. Ordinary the prisoner (Nerve) He tells what he knows (the GM decides how much is true). Nothing. He lies, and is believed.
Command Drive a hard task: Get men to do something hard and tiring: dig all night, march on after dark, cross a river. Ordinary — Done. Done slowly, or only half. They refuse.
Command Keep order: Stop plunder, drinking or a mutinous mood. Hard — They obey. Some slip away to it. They turn on him.
Letters Read or write: Read an order, a letter or a map's names; write a report. Easy — Read or written. Slowly, or with mistakes. He gets it wrong and does not know it.
Letters Forge a pass: Make a pass, an order or a billeting ticket that will be believed. Hard whoever checks it (Watch) It passes. Doubted: Talk past a guard instead. Seen through: held as a deserter or a spy.
Craft Mend kit: Mend a weapon, harness, boots, a cart or a radio set; a day's work. Ordinary — Mended. Not yet: another day. Ruined.
Craft Make something: Make ladders, a raft, a shelter, snowshoes or a litter from what is to hand. Ordinary — Made. Takes twice as long. It fails when it is used.
Ride Ride hard: Outride a pursuer, or catch a man who rides away. Ordinary the pursuer or the pursued (Ride) Away, or caught. Still close. Thrown: roll a fall as a wound.
Ride Swim a horse: Cross a deep ford or swim a river mounted. Hard — Across. Turned back. Swept away: Endurance check or drowned.
Fieldcraft Track: Follow men or animals. Ordinary the men being followed (Stealth) On their trail. Lost it. On the wrong trail.
Fieldcraft Find the way: Cross country without roads or a guide; at night, hard. Ordinary — On the way. Half a day lost. Lost: a day, or into the enemy.
Fieldcraft Hunt or gather: Find food or water for himself in the country. Ordinary — Fed today: no keep to pay. Nothing found. Something that makes him ill.
Watch Spot: See an ambush, a man hiding, a trap or a thing out of place. Ordinary whoever is hiding (Stealth) Seen. Missed. Sure there is nothing there.
Watch Search: Search a house, a body or a baggage wagon. Easy — Found what there is. Missed it. Missed it and left traces.
Stealth Sneak: Get past sentries, into a camp or away from one. Ordinary the sentries (Watch) Unseen. Seen, but not yet caught. Walks into them.
Stealth Steal: Lift a purse, a horse or rations unseen. Hard the owner or the guard (Watch) Taken. Not taken. Caught in the act: the provost.
Leechcraft Diagnose: Tell what a sick man has, and whether it will spread. Ordinary — Named: the GM tells which sickness. Unsure. Wrong.
Strength Force or carry: Force a door, lift a beam, carry a wounded man. Ordinary — Done. Not alone. Strained: a step of fatigue.
Agility Climb or jump: Climb a wall, jump a ditch, keep his feet on ice. Ordinary — Over. Not this way. Falls: roll a fall as a wound.
Endurance Endure: Keep going: swim, go without sleep, hold out in the cold. Ordinary — Holds out. A step of fatigue. Collapses, or goes under.
Wits Notice or remember: Recall a face, a road or a password; work something out. Ordinary — Yes. No. Remembers it wrong.
Nerve Keep his head: Stay calm out of a fight: under shelling in a dugout, at a hanging, before an officer. Ordinary — Steady. Shaken: −10 to his next check. Breaks: runs, freezes or lashes out.
Presence Impress: Stare a man down, make a first impression, be remembered. Ordinary the other man (Presence) He gives way. No effect. Made an enemy.

What becomes of a patron

For the Rules' Patrons.

Era d100
Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) 4% dies, 2% falls from favour, 3% changes sides, 4% disbands his regiment
Horse and musket (1775-1815) 3% dies, 1% falls from favour, 4% sells out or is posted
Crimean War (1854-1856) 5% dies, 1% falls from favour, 3% sells out or goes home
Civil War and frontier (1861-1876) 4% dies, 6% is dismissed by the examining board or resigns, 4% is promoted away
Plains nations (1860-1877) 3% dies, 3% loses his following

Wound tables

Each battle rolls its wounds on a table built from the record of that war, and these are the notes on where each one comes from. The tables themselves are in the printed tables and the wound roller. A gameplay-adjusted table is re-weighted from bone evidence to stand for every blow that landed, not only the ones that marked bone; an evidence table is the record itself.

Lützen 1632 - mass grave (bone evidence)

Battle injuries on 47 men buried in one grave at Lützen, most likely infantry of the Swedish Blue Brigade cut down by imperial cavalry. Killed only.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Counted from the study's tables of reliable battle injuries (69: 32 projectile, 21 blunt, 16 sharp), each weapon rolling on its own mechanism's injuries. Sides are as recorded; injuries the authors only call probable are left out. Where a bone could belong to more than one location (vertebra, ribcage, cranial base), it is shared by body exposure.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Nicklisch N., Ramsthaler F., Meller H., Friederich S., Alt K.W., 'The face of war: Trauma analysis of a mass grave from the Battle of Lützen (1632)', PLoS ONE 12(5): e0178252 (2017), open access (PMC5439951): Tables 1, 3 and 4.
  • Same study: lead balls in the grave were mostly from carbines (12-14), then muskets (5) and pistols (1-3); 21 men had gunshot wounds to the head; the attack came mainly from the front and side.
  • Injury tally: data/sources/lutzen-1632-mass-grave.csv.

Thirty Years' War - all hits (gameplay)

Where shot and blows land on a man in the open, before death and burial sort the evidence. For pike-and-shot battles of the 1600s.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of the Lützen dead and a stand-in for the wounded; the mix is from casualty totals of a later war.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Lützen 1632; the armies of The Swedish army (Swedes, Finns, Scots and Germans), The Imperial army and the Catholic League.

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 74.5% peninsular-1808-14-officers (wounded) + 25.5% lutzen-1632-mass-grave (killed), location by location.
  • No wounded records survive for the Thirty Years' War; the Peninsular War officers' wounds (same smoothbore lead balls and swords, 180 years later) stand in. Killed share as for the Napoleonic blend (about 1 killed to 3 wounded).

American Revolution 1775-83 - disabled veterans' wounds

Where Continental soldiers, militiamen and seamen were wounded, from the federal invalid pension lists of 1792-95. Men disabled for life who survived.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Counted wound by wound from 344 men's entries (379 wounds whose site is named; 32 more not located). Sides are recorded for about half and were close to even (85 left, 99 right), so left and right are pooled and split by body exposure (design estimate). 'Arm' without more detail is shared between upper arm and forearm.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Federal Revolutionary War Invalid Pension Claims, 1792-1795 (573 veterans), Magazine of Early American Datasets, University of Pennsylvania, 2021; from the Secretary of War's lists printed in American State Papers, Claims, vol. 1.
  • Wound-by-wound tally: data/sources/revolution-invalid-pensions-1792-95.csv. The weapon mix counts the 251 wounds whose cause is stated.

American Revolution 1775-83 - all hits (gameplay)

Where musket balls and shot land on a man in the open, before survival sorts the records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of a historical wounded table and a stand-in killed table; the mix is from casualty totals.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Cowpens 1781; the armies of The Continental Army (1775-1783), The British Army in America (1775-1783).

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 53.5% revolution-1775-83-pensioners + 46.5% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: Peckham, The Toll of Independence (1974), 7,174 Americans killed and 8,241 wounded in 1,331 land and 218 naval engagements (via Journal of the American Revolution, 'The 25 Deadliest Battles of the Revolutionary War', 2014).

Peninsular War 1808-14 - French officers' wounds

Where French officers were hit in Spain and Portugal, 1808-1814, by musket, sabre, bayonet, lance and cannon. Mostly men who survived.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Location counts are from the source (3,995 wound events). Each weapon rolls on its own recorded distribution (musket 2,848, sword 284, bayonet 97, lance 43, ordnance 209 wounds). Left and right are not recorded and are split evenly; 'arm' (bras) is put on the upper arm because wrist and forearm are listed apart. Rifles and pistols use the musket data.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Planas Campos J. and Grajal de Blas A., 'Wounds & Weapons in the Napoleonic War: a database of the Peninsular War', British Journal for Military History 7(3), Nov 2021, pp. 117-127: Table 1 (weapons, 4,359 entries), Table 2 (locations, 3,995 events), Tables 6-8 (location by firearm, edged weapon and ordnance). Source registers: French Army officer files, SHD 2Yb.
  • Same article, Table 11: 491 rank and file of the 100e de ligne - arms 22%, legs 40%, chest 6%, head 24%, abdomen 1%, shoulder 7% (officers: 26/44/4/14/3/9).
  • Comparison quoted there: Austrian officers wounded at Austerlitz (Guiga 2021) - upper limbs 26%, lower limbs 45%, head 6%, upper body 9%, back 4%.

Napoleonic era - all hits (gameplay)

Where musket balls and shot land on a man in the open, before survival sorts the records. Use for the Peninsula and Waterloo; the War of 1812 has its own table, built from the same records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of a historical wounded table and a stand-in killed table; the mix is from casualty totals.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Albuera 1811, Badajoz 1812; the armies of The British in the Peninsula (1808-1814), The French Empire in Spain (1808-1814).

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 74.5% peninsular-1808-14-officers + 25.5% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: about one killed for every three wounded in the Anglo-allied army at Waterloo (about 3,500 killed and 10,200 wounded; approximate, commonly cited totals).

War of 1812 - all hits (gameplay, borrowed records)

Where musket balls, rifle balls and shot land on a man in the open or in the woods, before survival sorts the records. No wound count survives for this war; the table is built from the Peninsular War records.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Borrowed: the Peninsular War wounded table blended with a stand-in killed table, at this war's own killed share.

Rolled by: the battlefields of Lundy's Lane 1814; the armies of The United States (1812-1815).

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 66.6% peninsular-1808-14-officers + 33.4% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: US forces lost about 2,260 killed in action and 4,505 wounded (commonly cited totals; British and Canadian losses are usually given only combined).
  • Peninsular War records: Planas Campos and Grajal de Blas, British Journal for Military History 7(3), 2021.

Crimean War 1855-56 - siege of Sevastopol, wounded (surgeons' returns)

British rank and file treated for wounds received in action from 1 April 1855 to the end of the war: almost all of it the siege of Sevastopol (the trenches, the Mamelon, the Redan). Men who reached a surgeon alive.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source: 6,984 gunshot wounds of known region (with 167 sword, bayonet and miscellaneous wounds left out). The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate). The 155 wounds of the larger arteries, nerves and joints of the limbs are shared between arms and legs as the other limb wounds are.

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Medical and Surgical History of the British Army which served in Turkey and the Crimea during the war against Russia in the years 1854-55-56 (London, 1858), vol. 2, Part II, Return No. 3 (p. 258) and the returns by region, Section II (pp. 286-339): non-commissioned officers and privates, 1 April 1855 to the end of the war - gunshot wounds of the head 851, face 533, neck 128, chest 420, abdomen (with gunshot fractures of the pelvis) 235, perineum and genito-urinary organs 55, back and spine 326, extremities 4,436 (upper 2,083, lower 2,198, with direct injury of the larger arteries 12 and nerves 22, and penetration of the larger joints 121 by difference); sword, lance and bayonet wounds 41 and miscellaneous wounds 126; 7,161 treated in all.
  • Same work, Return No. 1 (p. 257), for comparison: 14 Sep 1854 - 31 Mar 1855 (the Alma, Balaklava, Inkerman and the first winter's siege), head 206, face 125, neck 64, chest 158, abdomen 100, perineum 15, back and spine 84, extremities 1,763 of 2,515 gunshot wounds of known region (1,815 more unrecorded). Against this period the siege period has 1.5 times the share of head and of face wounds, 1.4 times the back, and fewer limb wounds (63.5% against 70.1%).

Crimean War 1854-56 - all hits (gameplay)

Where Minié bullets, musket balls and shell land on a man in the trenches and works before Sevastopol, before survival sorts the records. Built from the British surgeons' siege returns and a stand-in table for the killed.

How sure: a design estimate from analogous evidence. Blend of the historical siege wounded table and a stand-in killed table; the mix is from the war's killed and wounded totals.

Rolled by: the battlefields of The Great Redan, 18 June 1855, The Great Redan, 8 September 1855; the armies of British, French, Russian.

Sources:

  • Derived (tools/blend_tables.py): 81.7% crimea-1855-56-siege + 18.3% acw-1861-killed, location by location.
  • Killed share: 2,598 British rank and file killed in action in the whole war (Medical and Surgical History of the British Army ... in the Crimea, 1858, vol. 2, Concluding Observations) against 11,595 treated for wounds received in action (Returns Nos. 1 and 3: 4,434 and 7,161).

Civil War 1861-65 - wounded (surgeon's records)

Union soldiers treated for gunshot and shell wounds. Men who reached a surgeon alive.

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Rolled by: no battle here: it is the evidence the others are built from.

Sources:

  • Medical and Surgical History of the War of the Rebellion (1870-88), vol. 3, p. 392: head and neck 11%, chest and abdomen 18%, arms and hands 36%, legs and feet 35% of wounds (via Encyclopedia.com, 'Battlefield Wounds').
  • Same work: 35.6% upper extremities, 35.2% lower extremities (via Civil War Monitor, 'Wounded Warriors: Civil War Amputation').

Civil War 1861-65 - killed in action

Seat of the fatal wound in Union soldiers killed in action (n = 1,173).

How sure: taken directly from a source. Region totals are from the source. The split inside each region uses body exposure (design estimate).

Battlefields

Each battlefield lays out on the field map under Battlefield. What follows is what the field and its phases hold, and, briefly, what happened there.

Lützen, 16 November 1632

  • The armies: Swedes and Imperialists.
  • Fought for: the windmill battery, attacked by the Swedes.
  • The field: 220 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 2,200 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fog, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Thirty Years' War - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Lützen campaign, 1632 (Naumburg to Leipzig), at Lützen.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 541 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania in June 1630. He beat the Imperial and Catholic League armies at Breitenfeld in September 1631 and on the Lech in April 1632. The Emperor recalled Albrecht von Wallenstein to command. On 3 September 1632 Gustavus attacked Wallenstein's camp at the Alte Veste near Fürth and was beaten off.

Wallenstein then marched north into Saxony to join Heinrich Holk, hoping to drive the Elector of Saxony out of the war and draw the King after him. Leipzig fell at the start of November. Gustavus followed by forced marches and reached Naumburg.

On 14 November Wallenstein decided to go into winter quarters round Leipzig. He sent Pappenheim's corps west towards Halle. The next day the Swedes learned of it. Gustavus left Naumburg, took Weißenfels and, on 15 November, drove Isolani's Croats from the crossing of the Rippach. The delay cost him the daylight. His army spent the night in battle order in the open, about 2 km from Lützen. Wallenstein recalled Pappenheim at midnight and had his men dig along the Leipzig road through the night.

The places

  • Lützen: a small town on the road from Weißenfels to Leipzig. It anchored the Imperial right and was set on fire during the battle.
  • The Via Regia: the high road to Leipzig. Its ditches were deepened overnight and lined with Imperial musketeers.
  • The windmill hill: a low rise by Lützen with three windmills and the main Imperial battery.
  • The Floßgraben: a canal across the Swedish approach, which they had to cross before forming up.
  • The Rippach: the crossing between Weißenfels and Lützen where the Croats held the Swedes on 15 November.
  • Naumburg and Weißenfels: the Swedish base and the town taken on the march.
  • Halle: where Pappenheim was sent on 14 November, and from where he was recalled.
  • Leipzig: Wallenstein's base, and the road of his retreat.
  • The Schwedenstein: a boulder set up the day after the battle near where Gustavus fell. A chapel was built beside it in 1907.

The leaders

  • Gustavus Adolphus (Swedes, King of Sweden): led the cavalry of the right wing. He was killed.
  • Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar (Swedes, left wing): took over command when the King fell and led the late attack on the windmills.
  • Knyphausen (Swedes, second line): held the line with the reserve when the first line broke.
  • Nils Brahe (Swedes): commanded the infantry of the centre, according to Niderost.
  • Franz Albrecht of Saxe-Lauenburg (Swedes, with the King): rode with Gustavus when he was killed, and survived.
  • Albrecht von Wallenstein (Imperial, commander): fought on the defensive behind the road and withdrew in the night.
  • Gottfried Heinrich zu Pappenheim (Imperial, cavalry): aged 38. He rode back from Halle with his horse, was mortally wounded and died on the road to Leipzig.
  • Heinrich Holk (Imperial): led the counter-attack on the Swedish centre.
  • Ottavio Piccolomini (Imperial, cuirassiers): his horsemen fought on the Imperial left, where the King was killed.
  • Isolani (Imperial, Croat light horse): held the Rippach crossing on 15 November.

The battle

Fog lay over the ground on the morning of 16 November. The Swedes had formed by about 07:30, Niderost says, and held a service. The crossing of the Floßgraben and the fog slowed the deployment. The guns opened about 10:00, to little effect. About 11:00 the Swedish lines began their advance on the road.

On the Swedish right the King's horse drove the Imperial musketeers out of the road ditches and pushed back the cavalry beyond. Lützen was burning, and the smoke drifted across the centre. In the centre the Swedish brigades crossed the ditches. On the left Bernhard made little headway against the windmills.

Between 12:00 and 12:30 Pappenheim arrived with about 2,300 horse and struck the Swedish right. He was hit by a cannonball and musket balls, and was carried off. Holk counter-attacked in the centre. The Swedish brigades were driven back across the road with heavy loss. Both armies lost order, and the fighting broke into scattered firefights in the smoke and fog.

Some time after 13:00 Gustavus rode to help his foot. He was hit in the left arm. In the fog his small party ran into Imperial cuirassiers. He was shot in the back, stabbed and shot in the head. His body was found that evening among the dead on the Imperial side of the ditch. Knyphausen brought up the second line and held. Bernhard took command. By about 15:00 his first attack had failed and there was a lull.

The second phase is less well recorded. From about 15:30 the Swedes went forward again, retook the centre battery and, as the light failed, Bernhard's men took the windmill hill and its guns and turned them on the Imperialists. Fighting died down at dusk. About 18:00 Pappenheim's foot came up, about 2,900 strong, too late to attack. Wallenstein used them to cover his retreat, which began in the night. He left guns and baggage behind and more than 1,200 wounded, and fell back through Leipzig into Bohemia. The Swedes left the field about 11:00 the next morning.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The armies. Roberts gives the Swedes 18,996 men and 60 guns, and Wallenstein 16,770 men and 38 guns before Pappenheim's 2,300 horse came up. The Wikipedia summary gives the Swedes 18,738 and 60 guns and the Imperialists 19,175 and 43 guns; its text has Wallenstein at 13,000-15,000 before Pappenheim. Geijer says the King reckoned Wallenstein at 30,000.
  • The windmill battery. Niderost has 14 guns on the windmill hill.
  • The losses. The Wikipedia summary gives about 6,000 Swedish and 5,160 Imperial killed, wounded or taken; Roberts gives about 6,000 Swedish and an uncertain Imperial loss. Rickard gives 10,000 and 12,000. Nicklisch and her colleagues put the dead at 6,000-9,000.
  • The end of the day. Wikipedia has Wallenstein order the withdrawal about 17:00; Roberts has the retreat begin about 20:00.
  • Who won. The Swedes held the field and took the guns. Nicklisch and her colleagues note that the Imperialists took more Swedish colours, and say there was no clear victor. Wilson calls it a marginal Imperial tactical victory. Guthrie, quoted by Roberts, called it "a defeat for both sides".
  • The King's death. The accounts of it differ in detail. Schürger judges the page Leubelfing's account unreliable. Brzezinski argues the Swedes fought on because the news was kept from them.
  • The fog. Some writers think the smoke of burning Lützen made much of it.
  • The date. 16 November in the Gregorian calendar; 6 November in the Julian, used in Sweden at the time.

Forty-seven men

In 2011 archaeologists digging a trial trench on the north-east edge of Lützen, by the old Via Regia, found a pit 3.5 m by 4.6 m. It held 47 men, aged from about 15 to 50, most in their twenties. It was lifted out in two blocks of about 25 tonnes each and studied in Halle. More than half of the men had been hit by bullets, 21 of them in the head. Many carried old, healed injuries from earlier fights. Only five showed signs of a Scandinavian childhood. Nicklisch and her colleagues think most were foot of the Swedish Blue Brigade, caught by Imperial horse from the flank, though they say some may have been Imperial soldiers.

Question The accounts

Cowpens, 17 January 1781

  • The armies: Americans and British.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 120 by 100 hexes of 10 m, about 1,200 by 870 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the north-west.
  • Wounds: American Revolution 1775-83 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Cowpens campaign, 1781 (the Pacolet to the Broad), at Hannah's Cowpens.

The campaign

In 1780 the British took Charleston and beat the American southern army at Camden. Nathanael Greene took command of what was left in the autumn. With his army weak and the country round Charlotte stripped of food, he split it. On 21 December 1780 Daniel Morgan left Charlotte with about 600 men, Bearss says: Maryland and Delaware Continentals, Virginia militia and William Washington's dragoons. He went west, camped on the Pacolet at Grindal's Ford, and was joined by militia under Andrew Pickens.

Lord Cornwallis was getting ready to invade North Carolina. He feared Morgan would strike at the British post at Ninety Six. In early January 1781 he sent Lieutenant Colonel Banastre Tarleton after him, reinforced with the 7th Fusiliers, a troop of the 17th Light Dragoons and a second 3-pounder. Tarleton drove his men hard over swollen rivers. On 16 January he crossed the Pacolet, and Morgan fell back.

Morgan stopped that day at Hannah's Cowpens, a frontier grazing ground. The Broad River, in flood, lay about 6 miles behind him. He chose to fight rather than be caught crossing it. More militia joined him that afternoon. Tarleton woke his men at 02:00 on 17 January and marched through the dark.

The places

  • Hannah's Cowpens: a frontier grazing ground for cattle, where Morgan camped on 16 January.
  • The two rises: the gentle slope up which the British attacked, with the Continentals on the first crest and Washington's horse hidden behind the second.
  • The Green River Road: the road along which Tarleton fled towards Cornwallis's camp.
  • The Broad River: in flood about 6 miles behind Morgan, so that his men had nowhere easy to run.
  • The Pacolet River and Grindal's Ford: Morgan's camp in late December, and the river Tarleton crossed on 16 January.
  • Ninety Six: the British post in the backcountry that Cornwallis feared Morgan would attack.
  • Charlotte: where Greene split his army in December 1780.

The leaders

  • Daniel Morgan (Americans, commander): aged 45, a veteran of Quebec and Saratoga, and ill with rheumatism. He planned the battle in three lines.
  • John Eager Howard (Americans, the third line): commanded the Continentals and the Virginia men on the crest.
  • Andrew Pickens (Americans, the militia): commanded the second line of Georgia and Carolina militia.
  • William Washington (Americans, cavalry): commanded the Continental dragoons and the mounted militia held behind the rise.
  • McDowell and Cunningham (Americans, skirmishers): led the picked riflemen in front, about 60 each; Cunningham's were Georgians.
  • Banastre Tarleton (British, commander): aged 26, commander of the British Legion. He escaped.
  • Lord Cornwallis (British, commander in the South): not on the field. He heard the news that evening.
  • Robert Jackson (British, surgeon): gave Tarleton his horse when Tarleton's was shot, Bearss says.

The battle

Before dawn Morgan went among the militia. Thomas Young recalled him telling them to hold up their heads, and "three fires, and you are free". He drew up his men on the slope in three lines. In front were about 120 picked riflemen under McDowell and Cunningham, told to aim at officers and sergeants. About 150 yards behind them stood Pickens' militia, asked to fire two volleys and then fall back behind the Continentals. On the crest about 150 yards further back stood Howard's Continentals with Virginia militia and state troops. Washington's horse waited out of sight behind the second rise.

The British reached the field at sunrise, about 07:00, tired and short of food and sleep. Tarleton formed his light infantry, Legion foot and the 7th Fusiliers in line, with his two 3-pounders and 50 dragoons on each flank. The 71st Highlanders and about 200 Legion horse stood in reserve. He attacked at once. Young remembered the British line as "the most beautiful line I ever saw".

The riflemen fired and fell back on the militia. The militia fired and then went back round the Continentals' left. British dragoons rode at them, and Washington's horse came out and drove them off. Then the British foot came up the slope against Howard. For about 15 minutes, Bearss says, neither side gained ground.

Tarleton sent the 71st round the American right. Howard ordered the company on his right flank to face about and wheel to meet them. The men took it as an order to retreat and marched back, and the line went with them. Morgan rode up and asked why they were retreating. Howard said he was trying to save his right flank. The British, thinking the Americans beaten, came on in disorder. The Continentals halted, turned and fired at close range, then charged with the bayonet.

Washington's horse struck the British from the flank and rear, and the militia came back round the other flank against the Highlanders. The British foot and the 71st surrendered with their two guns. Tarleton tried to bring his reserve horse into the fight, but most of them rode away. With the few who stayed he charged Washington's horsemen, fought hand to hand, and escaped down the Green River Road. The fighting had lasted under an hour, and by 08:00 it was over. Morgan buried the dead and marched north with his prisoners. On 18 January Cornwallis wrote to Clinton that it was "impossible to foresee all the consequences that this unexpected and extraordinary event may produce".

Where the accounts disagree

  • The American army. Morgan reported about 800 men, two-thirds militia. The NPS gives at least 1,500, Mount Vernon about 1,000, and the American Battlefield Trust about 1,065. Babits, working from pension statements, puts it at about 2,000 (Wikipedia gives his figure as 1,887-1,912).
  • The riflemen. Bearss counts about 120 skirmishers; Mount Vernon about 150; Babits more than 300.
  • The British army. Morgan gave at least 1,150 with the baggage guard, and said British officers owned to 1,037 in action. Bearss gives nearly 1,100; Babits 1,250.
  • The British losses. Morgan reported about 110 killed, about 200 wounded and 531 prisoners. Bearss gives 110 killed and 830 prisoners, 200 of them wounded. The Trust gives 110 killed, 229 wounded and 529 taken.
  • The American losses. Morgan's returns give 12 killed and 61 wounded. Babits argues these covered only the Continentals; he gives about 25 killed and 124 wounded, and the NPS 24 and 120.
  • The militia. The common account, from Morgan's plan, has them fire two volleys and fall back in order. Babits says they fired at least five volleys at close range and were driven off by the bayonet.
  • The mistaken order. Bearss names Wallace's Virginia company as the one told to face about. Babits says Howard was outflanked and tried to turn a company against the Highlanders.
  • The night march. The NPS and Lieutenant Mackenzie have Tarleton start at 02:00; Bearss has him call in his pickets at 03:00.
  • Washington and Tarleton. The NPS, Mount Vernon and the Trust all describe a fight between the two. Mount Vernon has Tarleton shoot Washington's horse; the Trust has Tarleton's own horse shot. Wikipedia notes that Tarleton never mentioned a duel, was not wounded, and that the story may not be true.

His seventeenth birthday

Thomas Young turned 17 on the day of the battle. He rode with Major Benjamin Jolly's South Carolina mounted militia. When they came out of the woods, he wrote, "We made a most furious charge", through the British horse and back into their rear. He followed the rout for about 20 miles until his horse gave out. A British patrol caught him. He fought, and was cut about the hand, arm, forehead, shoulders and head. A loyalist who knew him tried to kill him, and British dragoons drove the man off. Tarleton had his wounds dressed. That night Young slipped away in the dark with another prisoner.

Albuera, 16 May 1811

  • The armies: Allies and French.
  • Fought for: the heights south of the allied line, attacked by the French.
  • The field: 150 by 230 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,990 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Overcast, breeze.
  • Wounds: Napoleonic era - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Albuera campaign, 1811 (Badajoz to Santa Marta), at La Albuera.

The campaign

In spring 1811 Marshal Beresford, with about 23,000 British and Portuguese, besieged French-held Badajoz on the Guadiana. Marshal Soult, commanding in Andalusia, stripped his garrisons to gather just under 25,000 men to relieve it: the 5th Corps, Latour-Maubourg's cavalry and two borrowed brigades under Godinot and Werlé. He left Seville at midnight on 9-10 May. Spanish patriots passed the news on, and it reached Beresford on 12 May.

Beresford took the 2nd Division and Hamilton's Portuguese to Valverde, covering the roads to Badajoz, and met General Blake, whose Spanish army was coming up to join him. On 15 May, sure that Soult was on the main road, he moved to La Albuera, where the road crosses a low ridge.

That afternoon the allied cavalry under General Long fell back across the Albuera stream too fast, giving up the far bank and its woods, and Beresford gave the cavalry to General Lumley. Blake's divisions arrived about 23:00 and camped in the dark. Cole's 4th Division marched from Badajoz at 02:00 and arrived at 06:30, without Kemmis's brigade, cut off by a rising river. Soult's infantry marched from Santa Marta before dawn. He believed Blake had not yet joined.

The places

  • Badajoz: the French-held fortress on the Guadiana; the siege was raised on 15 May and resumed on 19 May.
  • Valverde: where Beresford waited from 13 May, covering the roads to Badajoz, and met Blake.
  • Santa Marta: where Long's cavalry was pushed back on 15 May and Soult's infantry camped that night.
  • La Albuera: a large village on a knoll in front of the ridge, held by Alten's two German battalions.
  • The Albuera stream: formed just south of the village where the Nogales and Chicapierna brooks meet. In May it was a trickle, fordable almost anywhere.
  • The olive woods: on the French bank. With a low wooded hill between the brooks, they hid Soult's march round the allied right.
  • The heights: bare, rolling ground 60 to 150 feet above the water. The main fighting was in a dip about a mile south of the village.
  • Jerumenha: the crossing Kemmis's brigade had to use, about 30 miles round; it arrived the day after the battle.

The leaders

  • William Carr Beresford (Allies, commander): a British general and marshal of the Portuguese army, which he had reformed. He kept his troops hidden behind the crest.
  • Joaquín Blake (Allies, Spanish commander): about 14,000 men; slow to turn his line to face the flank attack.
  • José de Zayas (Allies, Spanish division): his four battalions turned to face the French on the heights and held for over an hour.
  • William Stewart (Allies, 2nd Division): sent Colborne's brigade into the attack before the rest of the division was up.
  • John Colborne (Allies, 1st Brigade): his brigade was ridden down by the lancers.
  • Daniel Hoghton (Allies, 2nd Brigade): killed as his brigade stood in line.
  • Lowry Cole (Allies, 4th Division): advanced on his own decision, urged by Colonel Henry Hardinge of the Portuguese staff.
  • Nicolas Soult (French, commander): planned the feint at the village and the march round the allied right.
  • Jean-Baptiste Girard (French, 5th Corps): led the two divisions of the turning column in one deep mass.
  • Victor de Latour-Maubourg (French, cavalry): sent in the lancers and hussars against Colborne's flank.

The battle

About 08:00, by one modern account, Godinot's 3,500 men attacked the village, while Werlé's brigade and the dragoons showed at the edge of the woods. Meanwhile Girard's and Gazan's divisions swept round through the olive groves, crossed both brooks and came up onto the heights beyond the allied right. Loy's Spanish horse gave way before their cavalry.

Beresford asked Blake to throw a line back across the heights. Blake sent only four battalions of Zayas's division and one battery. Girard came on in a column as wide as Zayas's line and four times as deep, 8,400 men in all. At about 60 yards the two sides opened fire.

Stewart, told only to support the Spaniards, sent Colborne's brigade straight in, each battalion as it arrived. Their fire, with four guns of Cleeves's battery, struck the French flank, and the French began to give way. Then a squall of rain and hail blew in from the north. In it, about 800 horsemen, Colonel Konopka's 1st Vistula Lancers and the 2nd Hussars, came round the open flank. Oman says three battalions were nearly destroyed within five minutes. Only the 2/31st formed square. Some lancers rode on into Beresford's staff; Beresford parried a lance and threw the man from his horse.

Zayas held. Hoghton's and Abercrombie's brigades took the Spaniards' place, and Gazan's division relieved Girard's. For about half an hour Hoghton's three battalions stood two deep against the 5th Corps at short range. Hoghton was killed. Colonel Inglis of the 57th, hit by grapeshot, lay in front of his men and called on them to "die hard". Neither commander sent in his reserve.

Cole then advanced without orders. Harvey's Portuguese beat off Latour-Maubourg's dragoons with volleys. Myers's three fusilier battalions met Werlé's 5,600 men in deep columns, and for perhaps 20 minutes they fired at 30 or 40 paces until Werlé's men broke. Myers was killed. Abercrombie's brigade wheeled into the flank of the 5th Corps, and the whole French mass went back over the Chicapierna, covered by its cavalry.

Beresford would not storm Soult's guns on the hill between the brooks, and another downpour ended the fighting. Both armies stood on 17 May. Soult left before dawn on 18 May, leaving several hundred badly wounded in a chapel in the wood.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The armies. Oman puts the allies at about 35,000 (10,449 British and Germans, 10,000 Portuguese, 14,000 Spaniards) and Soult at about 24,000. British Battles gives 32,000 and 23,000.
  • The losses. Oman counts 4,159 British, 389 Portuguese and 1,368 Spanish killed, wounded and missing. For the French, Soult reported 2,800, a return of 6 July 5,936, and Belmas and Lapène 7,000; Oman, from the officers hit, reckons about 7,900.
  • Colborne's brigade. Oman counts 1,248 lost of 1,648 in the three battalions ridden down, and 1,400 of about 2,000 for the brigade. He gives the lancers' loss as 130 of 580; Lieutenant Wojciechowski of the lancers recalled about 200 men and 16 officers.
  • The wounded. Oman believes British accounts that the lancers speared men on the ground, such as Major Brooke of the 2/48th after he surrendered. The Polish memoirs do not mention it.
  • The colours. Oman says five of the brigade's six colours were lost. Sorando, using French records, counts six taken, though part of the Buffs' cloth was saved.
  • Stewart's attack. Beresford said he meant the whole division to form behind Zayas first, and that Stewart refused Colborne's request to put a wing in square. Colborne's own letter says only that the order was not his.
  • Who decided the battle. Napier credits Hardinge with sending Cole forward, and writes that "the guidance of a commanding mind was nowhere seen". Oman calls Napier's account fine writing but full of errors born of his dislike of Beresford.
  • The times. British Battles has Godinot's attack at about 08:00. Oman's two battle plans are marked about 10:00 and about 11:30.

Under his body

Lieutenant Matthew Latham of the Buffs was near the King's Colour when the lancers came out of the hail. The ensign carrying it, Walsh, was 16; the other colour was carried by Ensign Edward Thomas, 15, who was killed by a lance after refusing to give his flag to a French officer. Latham took the King's Colour and fought for it with his sword. He lost an arm, and was knocked down and kicked by the horses. On the ground he tore the cloth from the staff and lay on it. At the end of the day Sergeant Gough of the 7th Fusiliers found it under him, stained with blood. Latham lived. His fellow officers gave him a medal, and a piece of the regiment's silver, the Latham Centrepiece of 1872, records the moment.

Badajoz, 6-7 April 1812 (the breaches and the castle)

  • The armies: Allies and French.
  • Fought for: the town of Badajoz, attacked by the Allies.
  • The field: 90 by 80 hexes of 10 m, about 900 by 690 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air, night.
  • Wounds: Napoleonic era - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Albuera campaign, 1811 (Badajoz to Santa Marta), at Badajoz.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 150 exchanges (a minute each).

What happened

After three weeks of siege the guns made two breaches, and a third in a day more. At ten at night on 6 April the 4th and Light Divisions went at the breaches. The ditch before the Trinidad had been flooded, the Light Division lost its way against a ravelin, and on the breaches sword blades, spiked planks, mines and the fire of men with three muskets each held them: some forty attacks failed, about two thousand fell in under two hours. Meanwhile Picton's 3rd Division crossed the Rivillas and took the castle by escalade, and the 5th Division got over the walls at San Vicente, off this map, and came along the ramparts; the French left the breaches, and Philippon surrendered at seven in the morning. The sack lasted until the next day.

How the field is drawn

The storm of Badajoz, 6-7 April 1812, the breaches and the castle, at 10 m a hex: 90 x 80 hexes, about 900 m east to west and 690 m north to south, north at the top: the town behind its south face, the Santa Maria bastion (left) and the Trinidad (right) with the three breaches, the castle on its hill at the top right, the Rivillas and its inundation down the east side, the glacis and the trenches below. Schematic, drawn by hand to the accounts (project doc badajoz-research), not traced from a plan. The walls are stone-wall edges with a deep ditch outside them (ladders go down into it); each breach is rubble with spiked planks (stakes) on its slope and the sword blades (a palisade edge) across its top; the ditch before the Trinidad is flooded. Wall heights, the ditch's depth, the breaches' widths, the divisions' strengths and the garrison's split are ours: no source reached gives them. Each storming party is 500 with ladders, as the plan of attack gave it.

Lundy's Lane, 25 July 1814

  • The armies: Americans and British.
  • Fought for: the British guns on the crest by the churchyard, attacked by the Americans.
  • The field: 130 by 110 hexes of 10 m, about 1,300 by 950 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the south-west.
  • Wounds: War of 1812 - all hits (gameplay, borrowed records).
  • On the travel map: Niagara campaign, 1814 (Fort Erie to Fort George), at Lundy's Lane.
  • The record: the fight lasted about 271 exchanges (a minute each).

The campaign

On 3 July 1814 Major General Jacob Brown crossed the Niagara near Lake Erie with about 3,500 Americans and took Fort Erie. Two days later Brigadier General Winfield Scott's brigade beat Major General Phineas Riall's British at Chippawa. Riall fell back to Fort George. Brown followed as far as Queenston, but he had no heavy guns for the forts, and Commodore Chauncey's squadron on Lake Ontario never came.

On 24 July Brown fell back to Chippawa to secure his supplies. Riall followed and took post at Lundy's Lane, about 4 miles north, on a low hill above the falls. Lieutenant General Gordon Drummond sailed from York, reached Niagara at daybreak on 25 July and took command. He sent Lieutenant Colonel John Tucker south from Fort Niagara along the American bank to press Brown.

Brown answered by sending Scott north towards Queenston, to counter the threat to the American bank. Riall ordered a retreat and sent Colonel Hercules Scott's brigade towards Queenston. Drummond countermanded both orders and hurried his troops to the hill.

The places

  • Lundy's Lane: the road west from the Portage road over the hill; the British line stood along it.
  • Drummond Hill: the rise above the lane, with a meeting house and burying ground where the British guns stood; now Drummond Hill Cemetery.
  • The Portage road: the main road north and south along the river, by which Scott came up from Chippawa.
  • Willson's tavern: on the Portage road, where the British pickets were chased away as Scott came up.
  • Chippawa: the American camp from 24 July, behind the creek where they had won on 5 July.
  • Bridgewater: the American headquarters, about 2 miles off, which gave the battle its American name. The British called it Niagara Falls.
  • Queenston: below the escarpment, where Brown had camped and Drummond fell back after the battle.
  • Fort George and Fort Niagara: the British forts at the mouth of the river.
  • Fort Erie: the American foothold on the Canadian bank, where Brown's army went afterwards.

The leaders

  • Jacob Brown (American, commander): came up with the main body after dark; wounded, he ordered the retreat at midnight.
  • Winfield Scott (American, 1st Brigade): attacked the hill without waiting, and was badly wounded late in the night.
  • Thomas Jesup (American, 25th Infantry): led his regiment round the British left in the dusk.
  • Eleazer Ripley (American, 2nd Brigade): held the crest and commanded after Brown and Scott were hit.
  • James Miller (American, 21st Infantry): took the British guns with the bayonet.
  • Peter B. Porter (American, volunteers and militia): led the third brigade, about 550 men.
  • Gordon Drummond (British, commander): born in Quebec, lieutenant governor of Upper Canada. He was shot in the neck and stayed in the field.
  • Phineas Riall (British, advance division): wounded in the arm and taken prisoner in the dusk.
  • Hercules Scott (British, 1st Brigade): his column, sent towards Queenston and back, reached the field about 21:00.
  • Joseph Morrison (British, 89th Foot): commanded the troops Drummond brought from Fort George.

The battle

Scott's brigade, about 1,000 men with Towson's battery, came up the Portage road in the early evening. Drummond says the action began at six. He had formed on the hill: the 89th, the Royal Scots and the 41st's light companies behind the crest, two brass 24-pounders on top, the Glengarry Light Infantry on the right and the militia on the left. Scott attacked rather than wait for Brown, and his brigade was cut up in the open in front of the guns.

On the British left, Major Jesup's 25th Infantry found a track round the flank. It drove back the light company of the 8th and the Incorporated Militia, and in the dusk took a group of wounded men and messengers behind the British line. Riall was among them, with the militia captain William Hamilton Merritt.

About 21:00 Brown came up with Ripley's brigade and Porter's volunteers, and they relieved Scott's men. Drummond had drawn his centre back, and the guns stood exposed. The 21st Infantry under Lieutenant Colonel Miller came up through cover in the dark, fired one volley at a few yards and charged. They took the guns and drove the British centre off the hill. At about the same time Hercules Scott's tired column came onto the field and ran into Ripley's brigade.

Drummond counter-attacked three times to win back the guns. The first was beaten off at short range. In the second, Scott led the remnant of his brigade in an attack of his own. It came under fire from both sides and broke, and he was badly wounded. The third came shortly before midnight, and at one point the lines met with the bayonet. It too was beaten off.

By midnight only about 700 Americans stood in line, and Brown and Scott were both disabled. Short of water and ammunition, Brown ordered Ripley back to Chippawa. They left the British guns, though they took one 6-pounder. At daybreak Ripley marched back with about 1,200 men, found Drummond on the hill with about 2,200, and withdrew. The Americans fell back to Fort Erie, where Drummond besieged them in August.

Where the accounts disagree

  • When it began. Drummond says six. Bonnycastle and the Lundy's Lane Historical Society's 1912 memorial say 17:30. Mansfield's life of Scott says about 40 minutes before sunset. Lieutenant Charles Anderson of the Provincial Artillery Drivers wrote of fighting from 16:00. The Niagara Falls museums have Scott leaving the woods shortly after 19:00.
  • The armies. The American Battlefield Trust gives 2,500 Americans and 3,500 British. The 1912 memorial gives about 4,000 Americans and 3,000 British. Bonnycastle claimed the Americans had 5,000.
  • The losses. The British return gave 84 killed, 559 wounded, 42 prisoners and 193 missing; the American return of 30 July, 171 killed, 572 wounded and 117 missing. Graves revises the prisoners and missing to 169 and 55 British, and the American figures to 174 killed, 79 prisoners and 28 missing. Bonnycastle has 870 British and 930 American killed and wounded.
  • Riall's capture. Drummond writes that Riall was taken by American cavalry as he was led to the rear. Modern accounts give the credit to Captain Ketchum's light company of the 25th Infantry.
  • Who sent Miller. Most accounts have Brown give the order, and Miller answer "I'll try, sir". Brown's own report, as summarised by the editors of the Madison papers, has Ripley order Miller forward.
  • The guns. Drummond says he took two American pieces but lost one in a mix-up in the dark. Graves blames the loss of the British guns on Drummond's failure to screen them with light troops.
  • The next morning. Drummond says the Americans abandoned their camp, threw their baggage into the rapids and burned Street's mills. Anderson says the British held the hill until about 10:00 and then withdrew to Queenston.
  • Who won. Both sides claimed it. Parks Canada says the Americans failed to drive the British off, which ended their offensive in Upper Canada. Barbuto calls it a British strategic victory. Brown blamed Ripley for not going back for the guns; Ripley asked for a court of inquiry.

I'll try, sir

James Miller commanded the 21st Infantry at Lundy's Lane. In the dark, with Scott's brigade worn out in front of the British guns, he was asked whether he could take them. His answer was "I'll try, sir." The 21st came up through a thicket on the flank of the battery. At a few yards' range they fired one volley, which put down most of the gunners, then went in with the bayonet. The guns were taken and held through three counter-attacks. Miller was made a brevet brigadier general from the day of the battle, and Congress voted him a gold medal in November 1814.

The accounts to choose

Where the sources disagree on something the battle turns on, the field map asks which account to fight (or rolls it, each as likely). The first is the game's own, and the enemy commander's benchmark is run on it; a battle on another is scored against history only.

Question The accounts
When did Scott attack the hill? Shortly after 19:00 (the Niagara Falls museums; Mansfield: about 40 minutes before sunset) (the game's own); At six (Drummond); At 17:30 (Bonnycastle and the 1912 memorial)
How many Americans? About 2,500 (the American Battlefield Trust) (the game's own); About 4,000 (the 1912 memorial); 5,000 (Bonnycastle, a single report)
How many British? About 2,600, the game's figure (the game's reading) (the game's own); About 3,000 (the 1912 memorial); About 3,500 (the American Battlefield Trust)

The Great Redan, 18 June 1855

  • The armies: British and Russians.
  • Fought for: the Redan's salient, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 100 by 105 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 910 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air.
  • Wounds: Crimean War 1854-56 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Siege of Sevastopol, 1855 (Kamiesh to the Chernaya), at the Great Redan.

The campaign

In 1854 Britain, France and the Ottoman Empire were at war with Russia. Their aim in the Crimea was Sevastopol, the base of the Russian Black Sea fleet. The allies landed near Eupatoria, north of the town, from 14 September 1854, and beat Menshikov's army on the River Alma on 20 September. They then marched round the town and laid siege to it from the south, the British supplied through the harbour at Balaklava. Meanwhile the Russians, under their engineer Eduard Todleben, dug a line of earthen batteries and took the guns and crews of their ships ashore.

The first bombardment opened on 17 October 1854. The Russian field army then attacked twice and failed: at Balaklava on 25 October, where the Light Brigade lost 247 of its 673 men, and at Inkerman, in fog, on 5 November. Then came winter. A storm on 14 November wrecked about 30 supply ships, the road from Balaklava turned to mud, and by February 1855 the British were down to about 12,000 men fit for duty (National Army Museum).

In May 1855 Pélissier replaced Canrobert in command of the French. On 7 June the French took the Mamelon and the British the Quarries, works in front of the Malakoff and the Great Redan. The fourth bombardment opened on 17 June. Next morning the French were to storm the Malakoff and the British the Redan.

The places

  • The Great Redan: the Russian Third Bastion, a V-shaped earthwork pointing south, with a ditch and an abatis, a fence of felled trees, in front.
  • The Malakoff: the earthwork on the hill east of the Redan, the main French objective.
  • The Quarries: the Russian works taken on 7 June. Campbell's column formed behind their parapet.
  • The Karabelnaya: the suburb behind the Redan and the Malakoff.
  • The Lancaster Battery: on the Victoria Ridge, where Pélissier went to give the signal.
  • The cemetery by Dockyard Creek: west of the Redan, taken by Eyre's brigade and given up that night.
  • Cathcart's Hill: the British burial ground, where Sir John Campbell was buried.

The leaders

  • Lord Raglan (British, commander): 66. He watched from the trenches, in the line of fire. He died of dysentery on 28 June.
  • Sir John Campbell (British, left column): had commanded the 4th Division until 7 June, then volunteered to lead its men. Killed.
  • Lacy Yea (British, right column): colonel of the 7th Royal Fusiliers, whom he had led at the Alma. Killed at the abatis.
  • Colonel Shadforth (British, 57th): led Campbell's storming party. Killed.
  • Aimable Pélissier (French, commander): chose to attack at 03:00 without the further bombardment Raglan wanted.
  • General Mayran (French, right division): went in early and was mortally wounded.
  • Eduard Todleben (Russian, chief engineer): had the works repaired in the night, and set field guns on the Malakoff.
  • General Khrulev (Russian): commanded the infantry in the Karabelnaya.

The battle

The bombardment of 17 June went on through the night, with mortars only. Under it, Kinglake says, the Russians repaired their batteries.

Pélissier was late. Before he reached the Lancaster Battery, General Mayran, on the far right, saw a fuse shine out in the dark and took it for the signal. His leading brigade went in a little before 03:00 against the works east of the Malakoff. It was driven back by grape, musketry and six steamers firing from the harbour, and Mayran was mortally wounded. The divisions of Brunet and d'Autemarre went in late and one at a time. Some got into the Karabelnaya and the Gervais Battery, but no support reached them and they were driven out.

Raglan watched the French checked. He felt it his duty, he wrote, to help them. He sent his two flank columns in without bombarding the Redan first. Each had 100 riflemen in front, 12 engineers, about 170 or 180 sailors and soldiers with ladders and wool-bags, 400 men to storm and 800 in reserve. The signal was a flag waved three times.

Campbell's column had 470 yards to cross. The riflemen and the ladder party went out ahead of the main body, into grape and musketry from the Redan's western face. Lieutenant Gerald Graham took the ladders on with the sailors. The 57th found the trench blocked by soldiers who had slipped away from their camps to join in. They filed out at the far end of the parapet, under fire from the Redan and the Artakoff Battery. Campbell and Shadforth were killed almost at once.

On the other flank, Yea's column met what Raglan called "such a shower of grape" as he had never imagined. The survivors of the covering party reached the abatis, some 80 yards from the work. The engineer A'Court Fisher found it scarcely damaged. Yea came up with his sword drawn and was shot dead. Fisher had the 150 or so men left lie down and wait. No supports came, and he ordered them back.

To the west, Eyre's brigade of about 2,000 men took the cemetery and some houses, about 07:00 by the Russian account, and withdrew that night. Pélissier pulled his men back at 07:00 or a little later, says Kinglake. Kinglake counts 62 officers and 717 men killed or wounded at the Redan, among them 52 of the 120 sailors.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The French start. Raglan and Pélissier set the attack for 03:00. Kinglake has Failly's brigade of Mayran's division go in "a little before three o'clock", after Mayran took a fuse for the signal. The Wikipedia article says the French went in nearly an hour early.
  • The ground to cross. Kinglake gives 400 yards to the Redan's point and 470 to the re-entering angle; the National Army Museum, about 250 yards.
  • The columns. Raglan's despatch names three columns, the centre aimed at the salient, but only the two flank columns went out. Kinglake gives each about 1,300 bayonets. The Wikipedia article speaks of 10 battalions.
  • British losses. Behan's Bulletins (1856) give 1,433 for the whole day: 155 killed, 1,126 wounded and 152 missing. Airapetov gives 1,728. The National Army Museum says over 1,500. Kinglake's 779 counts only the two Redan columns.
  • Russian losses. Russell (1865) gives 4,352 for the day, the bombardment and the French attacks included. Airapetov gives more than 4,818.
  • When the French withdrew. Kinglake says 07:00 or a little later; Pélissier's report, 08:30.

Anyone he spoke to

Lieutenant A'Court Fisher was the engineer officer with Yea's column. At the abatis he went to Colonel Yea and asked whether he should go on. Yea was shot dead before he could answer. Fisher turned to Captain Jesse of the Engineers, who was hit in the head and killed. He asked other officers in turn, and each was hit. At last he looked for any unhurt officer of the rank of captain and found none. He decided that he, a lieutenant, was the senior officer present, and called to the men to get back to the trenches "the best way you can" (Kinglake).

How the field is drawn

The first British assault on the Great Redan, Sevastopol, 18 June 1855, at dawn, at 10 m a hex: 100 x 105 hexes, about 1000 m east to west and 910 m north to south, north at the top: the Redan's point toward the British trench at the bottom, about 400 m away, the Karabelnaya suburb behind it. The work and the ground are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map (the point is cut off square, 120 m across, so that units in line can reach it); the deployment is our own reading, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The ditch is deep: without ladders it costs most of a move to cross; the ladder parties are marked as carrying ladders, and where they reach the ditch the ladders go down and it is crossed as an ordinary ditch.
