The Great Redan, 8 September 1855

  • The armies: British and Russians.
  • Fought for: the Redan's salient, attacked by the British.
  • The field: 100 by 80 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 690 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, strong wind from the north.
  • Wounds: Crimean War 1854-56 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: Siege of Sevastopol, 1855 (Kamiesh to the Chernaya), at the Great Redan.

The campaign

After 18 June the allies went back to digging. Lord Raglan died of dysentery on 28 June, and James Simpson, his chief of staff, reluctantly took command of the British. On the Russian side Admiral Nakhimov, a leader of the defence, was shot in the head by an allied marksman and died on 10 July.

On 16 August Gorchakov tried to break the siege from outside. He attacked the French and Piedmontese at the Traktir bridge on the Chernaya with some 58,000-60,000 men and was beaten off with the loss of about 8,800. After that the garrison could expect no relief, and the French trenches crept up until they were a few yards from the Malakoff.

The allies bombarded the town from 17 August and again, more heavily, from 5 September. At noon on 8 September the French would storm the Malakoff and the works either side of it. When they were established, the British would storm the Redan, and the French would go in against the town front further west.

The places

  • The Redan's salient: the point of the work, chosen by Simpson because it was "less exposed to the heavy flanking fire". The ditch there was about 15 feet deep.
  • The advanced parallel: the British forward trench, from which the stormers went over. Codrington watched from the fifth parallel.
  • The Malakoff: the work east of the Redan, taken by the French at noon and held.
  • The Mamelon: the French-held hill in front of the Malakoff, where Pélissier gathered his storming columns.
  • The Barrack Battery: Russian guns west of the Redan.
  • The raft bridge and the North Side: the floating bridge across the harbour by which the garrison left that night.

The leaders

  • James Simpson (British, commander): 63. He watched from the trench with his cloak over his head.
  • Sir William Codrington (British, Light Division): planned the attack with Markham of the 2nd Division.
  • Charles Windham (British, 2nd Division): led the assaulting column into the Redan. Known after as "Redan Windham".
  • Colonel Unett (British, 19th): senior officer of Shirley's brigade. Badly wounded before reaching the abatis.
  • Major Augustus Welsford (British, 97th): led half the ladder party. Killed.
  • Sir Colin Campbell (British, Highland Division): held the trenches that night, ready to attack again.
  • Aimable Pélissier (French, commander): watched from the French observatory on the right.
  • Patrice de MacMahon (French, 1st Division): took the Malakoff.
  • Mikhail Gorchakov (Russian, commander): withdrew the garrison to the North Side.
  • Colonel Ventsel (Russian, Vladimirski Regiment): ordered the counter-attack that cleared the Redan.

The battle

It was a cold day, with a strong wind and dust. At 10:30 the stormers of the Light and 2nd Divisions moved into the advanced parallels. Shortly before noon the French left their trenches in front of the Malakoff, crossed the few yards to it, and got in. The tricolour went up on its parapet. Simpson says this was the British signal.

The covering party went first: 100 men of the Buffs under Captain Lewes and 100 of the 2nd Battalion, Rifle Brigade, under Captain Hammond. Then came the ladders, 160 men of the Buffs under Captain Maude and 160 of the 97th under Welsford. The stormers followed, the Light Division leading. The guns of the Redan swept them with grape as they crossed. The British bombardment had torn up the abatis, and they got through it. But the ladders were too short, and some had been broken or left behind. Only six or seven reached the salient. Men jumped down into the ditch and climbed the parapet.

At first there was little opposition. The Russians fell back behind their traverses and a breastwork, and fired from there. Hammond and Welsford were killed. Two brigadiers, Shirley and Van Straubenzee, were put out of action. Of the senior officers, only Windham and Captains Fyers, Lewes and Maude got into the Redan unhurt.

Windham sent three officers back in turn for reinforcements. All three were wounded on the way. The supports came forward in disorder and crowded into the salient. Then Russian reserves came up from the town and drove the British back over the parapet into the ditch. Simpson says the fight lasted "nearly an hour".

Simpson meant to attack again next morning with the Highlanders under Sir Colin Campbell and the 3rd Division. About 23:00 the Russians began blowing up their magazines. A small party sent forward by Campbell found the Redan empty. The Russians crossed to the North Side by the raft bridge, then took it up, and sank their remaining warships. Campbell's men occupied the Redan at daylight on 9 September.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The signal. Simpson says the tricolour on the Malakoff's parapet. The eyewitness in Dickens's Household Narrative says four rockets fired from Chapman's attack, the British left, once the flag was seen. The Wikipedia article says the flag of St George raised over the Mamelon.
  • How long it lasted. Simpson says "nearly an hour", the Household Narrative "an hour". The Wikipedia article says Windham held the Redan for about 2 hours. The game follows Simpson.
  • The ground to cross. The British Empire site, following Collins, says the nearest parallel was nearly 300 yards from the Russian ramparts. The Wikipedia article calls it a 400 m field. The game gives about 200 yards.
  • The stormers. Simpson gives about 1,000 men, half from each division, besides the 200 covering and 320 with ladders. The Household Narrative lists 760 from the 2nd Division alone. The Wikipedia article counts about 11,000 men in the whole right attack.
  • British losses. The Wikipedia article gives 2,447: 385 killed, 1,886 wounded and 176 missing. Fletcher and Ishchenko give 390 killed, 2,043 wounded and 177 missing.
  • Russian losses. For the whole day Russell (1865) gives 11,692; Fletcher and Ishchenko, 11,666 (2,684 killed, 7,243 wounded, 1,739 missing).
  • The Russian counter-attack. The Wikipedia article has Ventsel send in the Selenginski and Iakutski regiments, about 3,000 men. The Kamchatski stood in the first line; the game follows Wikipedia for the counter-attack.
  • Windham. Simpson says he stayed with the troops throughout. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography says he went back himself to ask for men, found the retreat already ordered, and was criticised for it by soldiers, while William Howard Russell of The Times wrote that he had "saved the honour of the army".

Redan Massy

Lieutenant W. G. D. Massy of the 19th was about 17. His captain went down with cholera, and Massy led the Grenadier Company in the assault. He was the first of his regiment into the Redan, and few followed him. He stood on the rampart, in view of both sides, waiting for the men to come on, until he was hit in the leg. The Russians left him where he lay. That night, when they blew up the work, falling masonry crushed him. He was brought in the next day, nearly dead, and spent about six months in bed. The army knew him after as "Redan Massy". Brigadier Collins (1964) set his account against the Dictionary of National Biography, which implied that Massy had run.

How the field is drawn

The British assault on the Great Redan, Sevastopol, 8 September 1855, at 10 m a hex: 100 x 80 hexes, about 1000 m east to west and 690 m north to south, north at the top: the Redan's point toward the British trench at the bottom, the Karabelnaya suburb behind it at the top. The work, its ditch, the line either side, the breastwork, the trench, the ravines and the shell holes are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map (the point is cut off square, 120 m across, so that units in line can reach it); the deployment is just after noon, in our own words, with round numbers for play. The ditch is deep: without ladders it costs most of a move to cross; the ladder party is marked as carrying ladders, and where it reaches the ditch the ladders go down and it is crossed as an ordinary ditch.

The accounts to choose

Where the sources disagree on something the battle turns on, the field map asks which account to fight (or rolls it, each as likely). The first is the game's own, and the enemy commander's benchmark is run on it; a battle on another is scored against history only.

Question The accounts
How many stormers went in? About 1,000, half from each division (Simpson) (the game's own); About 1,760 (the Household Narrative's 760 from the 2nd Division, with 1,000 from the Light)
How long did the British hold the Redan? Nearly an hour (Simpson; the Household Narrative: an hour) (the game's own); About 2 hours (the Wikipedia article)

First Bull Run, 21 July 1861

  • The armies: Confederates and Union.
  • Fought for: the top of Henry Hill, attacked by the Union.
  • The field: 140 by 130 hexes of 10 m, about 1,400 by 1,130 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the south-west.
  • Wounds: Civil War 1861-65 - all hits (gameplay).
  • On the travel map: First Bull Run campaign, 1861 (Fairfax to Gainesville), at Henry Hill.

The campaign

In May 1861 the Confederate government moved to Richmond. The best road there from Washington ran through Manassas Junction, where the Orange & Alexandria Railroad met the line from the Shenandoah Valley. Beauregard held the crossings of Bull Run in front of the junction with about 20,000 men. Johnston had about 12,000 in the Valley.

Winfield Scott's plan was to press both at once: Patterson would hold Johnston while McDowell marched on Manassas. McDowell left Washington on 16 July with about 35,000 men, mostly new volunteers. His probe at Blackburn's Ford was beaten back on 18 July. While he scouted, Johnston slipped away from Patterson, and most of his brigades came by rail to Manassas on 20 and 21 July.

McDowell chose a flank march. Tyler's division would make a show at the Stone Bridge. Hunter and Heintzelman would go round by Sudley Ford and come down behind the Confederate left.

The places

  • Centreville: McDowell's base, about 5 miles from Bull Run.
  • The Stone Bridge: the Warrenton Turnpike's bridge over Bull Run, held at first by Evans.
  • Sudley Ford: where the Union flank column crossed Bull Run in the morning.
  • Matthews Hill: north of the turnpike, where the Confederates lost the morning fight.
  • Henry Hill and the Henry house: the plateau south of the turnpike and Young's Branch, where the Confederates rallied. The game's field.
  • Chinn Ridge: the next ridge west, beyond the Sudley road, where the last Union brigade was broken.
  • Portici (the Lewis house): Johnston's headquarters, later a field hospital.
  • Cub Run bridge: on the turnpike east of Bull Run, where an overturned wagon blocked the retreat.

The leaders

  • Irvin McDowell (Union, commanding): planned the flank march. George B. McClellan replaced him after the defeat.
  • Samuel P. Heintzelman (Union, division): led the Zouaves forward himself.
  • William F. Barry (Union, chief of artillery): sent the two regular batteries onto the hill and posted their supports.
  • Charles Griffin and James B. Ricketts (Union, regular batteries): Battery D, 5th US Artillery, and Battery I, 1st US Artillery. Ricketts was wounded and taken prisoner.
  • Joseph E. Johnston and P. G. T. Beauregard (Confederate, commanders): Johnston, the senior, fed reinforcements to the left; Beauregard ordered the general attack.
  • Thomas J. Jackson (Confederate, brigade): formed his Virginians and guns on the edge of Henry Hill, and got his name "Stonewall".
  • Arthur C. Cummings (Confederate, 33rd Virginia): a Virginia Military Institute man who had served in Mexico. He led the charge on Griffin's guns.
  • J. E. B. Stuart (Confederate, 1st Virginia Cavalry): guarded Jackson's left and rode into the Fire Zouaves.
  • Kirby Smith, Arnold Elzey and Jubal A. Early (Confederate, late brigades): Smith was wounded on arrival and Elzey took over. With Early they broke the Union right.

The battle

The flank column was slow and did not reach Sudley Ford until after 09:00. Evans, at the Stone Bridge, guessed Tyler was only making a show, and met the column on Matthews Hill about 10:15. Bee and Bartow came up about 11:00, but Union troops kept arriving, and by about 11:30 the Confederates were falling back over Young's Branch. Jackson says he posted his guns on the far edge of Henry Hill at 11:30. Johnston and Beauregard rode up about 12:30 and rallied the broken brigades behind him.

The game's field shows Henry Hill from about 14:00 to the break after 16:00. At about 14:00 McDowell sent Ricketts's and Griffin's batteries onto the hill near the Henry house, some 300 yards from Jackson's guns. Barry led up the Fire Zouaves (11th New York) in support, with the 14th Brooklyn and a battalion of Marines, most of them recruits of under three weeks. Union shells aimed at sharpshooters in the Henry house mortally wounded Judith Henry, a bedridden widow.

The Zouaves' first advance broke under a volley from the pines. Stuart at first took them for friends, then saw their flag and charged. Then the 33rd Virginia came out of the woods on the left. Griffin took them for Confederates and wanted to fire canister. Barry said they were the battery's supports (Joint Committee report, 1863). The Virginians' volley cut down gunners and horses. Griffin lost 27 of 95 men and 55 of 101 horses. Ricketts was wounded and his lieutenant, Ramsay, killed.

For about two hours the guns changed hands. Heintzelman says Ricketts's battery was taken and retaken three times. About 15:30 Jackson sent the 4th and 27th Virginia in with the bayonet and broke the Union centre. Sherman's regiments went up in turn. Colonel Cameron of the 79th New York was mortally wounded. Sherman says disorder spread through his brigade about 15:30.

On the left, Elzey, leading after Kirby Smith fell, drove Howard's tired brigade off Chinn Ridge. Early's three regiments, with Stuart and Beckham's battery, struck the Union right in flank while Beauregard attacked in front. Heintzelman says the retreat began about 16:30. When a wagon overturned on the Cub Run bridge, it became a rout among the carriages of spectators. The Confederates were too disordered to follow far. McDowell's army was back at Washington by 22 July.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The armies. The NPS gives McDowell 35,000 against Beauregard's 22,000 and Johnston's 10,000. The American Battlefield Trust, following Salmon and Livermore, gives 28,450 Union and 32,230 Confederate.
  • The losses. The Trust and the Davis booklet give 2,896 Union (460 killed, 1,124 wounded, 1,312 missing); the Union return, 2,708. The Trust gives 1,982 Confederate; Davis, nearly 2,000.
  • The guns taken. The NPS trail marker has the 33rd Virginia take two of Griffin's howitzers. Barry says ten guns were lost in all. Jackson claims seven besides the battery Cummings took and lost.
  • Stuart's charge. Stuart reports about 300 men fit for duty, half sent with Major Swann. Emerging Civil War (2021) puts the charge at about 150 horsemen.
  • The last attack. Johnston has Kirby Smith arrive about 15:00. Davis puts Howard's attack about 16:00 and Early's between 16:00 and 17:00. The older NPS handbook has the line break about 15:45.
  • The "stone wall". Bee was mortally wounded and left no report, so his words are uncertain. Burnett Rhett claimed he meant them as a reproach.
  • Judith Henry. The NPS gives her age as 84, Wikipedia 85. The NPS says artillery fire struck her; the Metropolitan Museum, gunshot wounds.

No words can describe

Captain James Ricketts was hit in the thigh beside his guns and taken prisoner. In Washington his wife Fanny heard only conflicting reports. On 25 July she set out for the Confederate lines, and that evening learned at their headquarters that he was alive. Next morning she reached Portici, the Lewis house, where the kitchen and hallways had become operating rooms. She nursed him and other wounded men there for about a week, and wrote in her journal that "no words can describe the horrors around me". When he was sent to prison in Richmond on 2 August, she went with him, and stayed until his release in December.

The hill, the branch, the woods and the ridge are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the early afternoon, in our own words, with round numbers for play.

The Fetterman Fight, 21 December 1866

  • The armies: US Army and Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho.
  • Fought for: no one place the map can mark.
  • The field: 150 by 120 hexes of 10 m, about 1,500 by 1,040 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, calm or light air from the north-west.
  • Wounds: Indian Wars 1865-71 - arrow wounds (US Army surgeons).
  • On the travel map: Fort Phil Kearny, 1866 (Red Cloud's War), at Fetterman battlefield.

The campaign

In 1863 John Bozeman opened a trail north from the North Platte, through the Powder River country, to the Montana goldfields. The Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho had taken this country from the Crow by about 1860 and hunted it.

In June 1866 commissioners called the Lakota to Fort Laramie to agree to safe passage on the trail. On 13 June Colonel Henry B. Carrington arrived there with the 18th Infantry, on his way to build forts along it. The next day the Oglala leader Red Cloud refused to deal with him and left, with They Fear Even His Horses and others. Carrington garrisoned Fort Reno on 28 June, began Fort Phil Kearny on the Little Piney in mid-July, and founded Fort C. F. Smith on 13 August.

By mid-December Shannon Smith counts nearly 70 soldiers and civilians dead in more than 50 fights. Captain William J. Fetterman arrived on 3 November. On 6 December, relieving a wood train, Lieutenant Horatio Bingham chased decoys and was killed with a sergeant. On 19 December Captain James Powell relieved another train and, as ordered, did not follow over Lodge Trail Ridge.

The Oglala, Miniconjou, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho camped on the Tongue River planned a large ambush before winter scattered them. They chose ground on the Bozeman Trail north of Lodge Trail Ridge, out of sight of the fort.

The places

  • Fort Phil Kearny: Carrington's headquarters, a stockade of 17 acres on the Little Piney, near present-day Story, Wyoming.
  • Pilot Hill: the lookout near the fort whose pickets signalled attacks on the trains.
  • Sullivant Hills: on the wood road, where the train was attacked on 21 December.
  • The pinery: the woods about five miles north-west of the fort, where the trains cut timber.
  • Lodge Trail Ridge: about two miles north of the fort. Carrington forbade pursuit over it.
  • Peno Creek: the creek and flats at the north foot of the ridge, where the warriors waited.
  • The rocks: boulders at the end of the fight nearest the fort, where most of the dead lay. A monument went up near them in 1908.
  • Fort Laramie: about 230 miles south-east, where John "Portugee" Phillips carried the news.

The leaders

  • Henry B. Carrington (US Army, commanding): colonel of the 18th Infantry. He was later blamed for the loss.
  • William J. Fetterman (US Army, captain): a brevet lieutenant colonel from the Civil War, who claimed the command by seniority. Killed.
  • Frederick H. Brown (US Army, captain): the quartermaster, about to be transferred. Killed.
  • George W. Grummond (US Army, lieutenant): led the cavalry, ordered to obey Fetterman and not leave him. Killed.
  • Red Cloud (Oglala Lakota): the leading voice for war. Wikipedia has him present, his role unknown; the fort's history doubts he fought.
  • High Back Bone (Hump) (Miniconjou Lakota): named as the chief fighting leader.
  • Crazy Horse (Oglala Lakota): by later tradition a leader of the decoys. Monnett finds no early Indian account that puts him there.
  • American Horse (Oglala Lakota): named by Ricker's informants as a decoy. He said he killed Fetterman.
  • Little Wolf (Cheyenne), Black Shield and Black Leg (Lakota), Medicine Man and Black Bear (Arapaho): other leaders named by the fort's history.

The battle

On 21 December, Carrington testified, "it was nearly 11 o'clock" when Pilot Hill signalled that the wood train had corralled under attack. He sent 49 infantry and 27 men of the 2nd Cavalry. Fetterman took the command from Powell. Brown and two civilians, James Wheatley and Isaac Fisher, with Henry repeating rifles, went too: 81 in all. The written order was "Under no circumstances pursue over the ridge viz; Lodge Trail Ridge."

Fetterman did not go west to the train but north-east, to the south end of Lodge Trail Ridge. Carrington's report first took this as a move against the attackers' rear. Ten decoys, two each from the Oglala, Miniconjou, Brulé, Cheyenne and Arapaho, drew the column along the crest towards Peno Creek. The cavalry went ahead and the infantry fell behind.

Carrington heard firing about 12:00. At a signal the warriors came up out of the ravines and across the flats. The cavalry fell back up the ridge. Wheatley, Fisher and a few soldiers held rocks at the far end and were killed there. The rest of the cavalry made a stand on the ridge and were overrun. The infantry, with Fetterman and Brown, made their stand at the rocks nearest the fort. The Miniconjou White Bull, then 17, told Stanley Vestal in 1932 that he pulled a wounded man out of the fight and killed a soldier with an arrow. Only six soldiers died of gunshots.

Captain Tenodor Ten Eyck went out with about 75 men and reached the ridge top about 12:45. The warriors drew off. His men brought back 49 bodies, "nearly all ... heaped near four rocks at the point nearest the Fort", Carrington says. The rest, Grummond among them, came in next day, stripped and mostly mutilated. Phillips and Daniel Dixon rode for help that night. Carrington was relieved in January 1867.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The warriors. Carrington's report says "probably three hundred"; his telegram, "nearly three thousand". Surgeon C. M. Hines guessed 4,000-5,000. Wikipedia gives about 1,000; a review of Monnett's 2017 book, more than 1,500.
  • Their losses. Ambrose gives 13, some hit by their own arrows; George Bent, 14. White Elk, a Cheyenne, said 2 Cheyenne and 50-60 Lakota. Red Cloud later named 11 Oglala dead.
  • The soldiers. Carrington gives 81; Smith counts 80.
  • The order of the fight. Ambrose has the infantry overrun first, the cavalry 20 minutes later. Smith and the fort's history have the cavalry caught first, the infantry last at the rocks. Vaughn found the infantry could not have reached the cavalry's ground in the time.
  • The sides of the trap. Wikipedia puts the Cheyenne and Arapaho west of the trail and the Lakota east. The game's map has them the other way round.
  • The boast. Legend has Fetterman say that with 80 men he could ride through the whole Sioux nation; WyoHistory's battlefield page says 100. Smith traces his reckless image to books by Carrington's two wives (1868, 1910); Monnett also treats it as myth.
  • The orders. The Carringtons say the order was given twice. Smith suggests the two men may have planned an attack from the rear.
  • Fetterman's death. Carrington found him and Brown each shot in the left temple, as if they shot each other. American Horse claimed to have killed him.
  • Crazy Horse. Monnett traces the decoy story to Mari Sandoz's 1942 book, though he doubts Crazy Horse was absent.

The bugler

Adolph Metzger was the cavalry's bugler, a German-born soldier who had served since 1855. Accounts say that at the end he fought with his bugle, striking out with it until it was battered out of shape. He is thought to have been the last soldier to die, though whether he fell with Wheatley and Fisher or near Fetterman is not clear. American Horse testified that the warriors did not mutilate his body. They covered his head with a buffalo robe. When Carrington's men came to collect the dead, his was the only body not cut. Nobody recorded why he was spared.

The ridge, the ravines, the rocks and the creek are drawn by hand to the shape the accounts give, not traced from any map; the deployment is the moment the decoys turned, in our own words, with round numbers for play. Question The accounts

The Wagon Box Fight, 2 August 1867

  • The armies: US Army and Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho.
  • Fought for: the wagon-box corral, attacked by the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho.
  • The field: 100 by 80 hexes of 10 m, about 1,000 by 690 m, north at the top.
  • The weather: Fair, breeze from the west.
  • Wounds: Indian Wars 1865-71 - arrow wounds (US Army surgeons).
  • On the travel map: Fort Phil Kearny, 1866 (Red Cloud's War), at Wagon Box corral.

The campaign

In July 1867 the Oglala under Red Cloud, other Lakota bands, Northern Cheyenne and a few Arapaho held their Sun Dance on the Tongue and Rosebud rivers. They then planned to strike the Bozeman Trail forts again. They could not agree which fort to attack first, and split. One party, mostly Cheyenne, went against Fort C. F. Smith. On 1 August it attacked a hay camp there, in the Hayfield Fight, and was beaten off. The other, mostly Lakota, went against Fort Phil Kearny.

The fort burned wood for building, cooking and the winter. Civilian contractors, Gilmore and Porter's men by WyoHistory's account, cut it in the pinery west of the fort, under an infantry guard. On 31 July Captain James Powell took Company C, 27th Infantry, out for a 30-day turn as the guard, 51 men by Wikipedia's count. The company had new Springfield breech-loading rifles, converted from muzzle-loaders, which could be fired much faster than the old muskets.

The contractors' men had made a corral of 14 wagon boxes taken off their running gear and set on the ground, about 60-70 feet by 25-30. Each box was about 10 feet long, 4½ feet wide and 2½ feet high, of planks about an inch thick. On the morning of 2 August, 14 soldiers were out escorting the wood wagons and 13 guarding the woodcutters' camp.

The places

  • Fort Phil Kearny: on the Little Piney, south-east of the corral; accounts give three to six miles. The relief came from here.
  • Pilot Hill: the fort's lookout, from which the fight was seen.
  • The pinery: the woods on the mountain slope where the wood was cut.
  • Big Piney and Little Piney creeks: the corral stood on the open ground between them. The woodcutters' camps were along both.
  • Sullivant's Ridge: the hill to the east where several hundred warriors watched.
  • The two sites: the place Sam Gibson pointed out in 1908, now marked by the 1921 and 1936 monuments, and a rival site marked with a pipe in 1916.
  • Fort C. F. Smith: the fort on the Bighorn where the other party fought the Hayfield Fight on 1 August.

The leaders

  • James W. Powell (US Army, captain, 27th Infantry): commanded at the corral and wrote the official report.
  • John C. Jenness (US Army, lieutenant): Powell's second. Shot in the head and killed.
  • Benjamin F. Smith (US Army, major): led the relief from the fort.
  • Samuel S. Gibson (US Army, 27th Infantry): aged 18, the youngest man in the corral. He wrote the fullest soldier's account.
  • Red Cloud (Oglala Lakota): the leader of the war. Jenness was said to have seen him on a hill through field glasses; WyoHistory calls his presence unverified.
  • Red Cloud's nephew (Oglala Lakota): led the main mounted charge, by WyoHistory's account. His name is not given.
  • High Back Bone (Hump) (Miniconjou Lakota) and Crazy Horse (Oglala Lakota): Ostlind names both as leaders of the attack.
  • Fire Thunder (Oglala Lakota): fought there, and later told John Neihardt of it.
  • White Bull (Miniconjou Lakota): mostly watched, by his own account to Stanley Vestal.

The battle

Gibson says the fight began about 07:00. He was on picket and saw seven mounted warriors coming over the divide from the north. More rose behind them. A party of about 200 on foot went for the mule herd. Others struck the woodcutters' camps and burned them. Three soldiers and four civilians were killed outside the corral. Powell went out at the attackers' rear, which let others reach the woods or the fort. Some warriors stopped to take the horses and mules, which gave the corral time. In the end 26 soldiers and 6 civilians were inside.

Within about 15 minutes, WyoHistory says, some 800 mounted warriors were round the corral. The first charge, from the south-west, met steady fire and turned away. The men fired through holes and over grain sacks, yokes and kegs piled between the boxes. They had about 7,000 rounds.

For about three hours the warriors came on foot. Some got within a few feet of the boxes. Gibson writes that the bullets tore the tops of the boxes "to slivers". Burning arrows set the hay and dung alight. Jenness was killed, with Privates Henry Haggerty and Thomas Boyle, and two men were wounded. WyoHistory has a mounted charge in a wedge, led by Red Cloud's nephew, between 12:00 and 13:00. Powell later said his ammunition was running low and his men worn out.

Smith left the fort with about 100 men and a mountain howitzer; Wikipedia says about 11:30. A shell fell short of the ridge, but the warriors drew off. Smith found most of the defenders alive. He said their faces looked as if blacked with "burnt cork". The fight had lasted about six hours. Fire Thunder later told Neihardt that the attack failed because the soldiers had new guns. Even so, the Lakota counted the day a success: they had burned the camps, taken the mules and killed soldiers.

Where the accounts disagree

  • The warriors' losses. Hyde, Vestal and several Sioux leaders say 6 killed and 6 wounded. Powell reported 60 killed and 120 wounded; Keenan calls this "wildly exaggerated". Soldiers who were there said 300-800. A Sioux told Colonel Richard Dodge in 1867 of 1,137 dead and wounded, and Grenville Dodge said Red Cloud gave him over 1,100 in 1885. Descendants at the 1969 re-enactment said 1,200-1,500.
  • The warriors. Gibson's comrade cried out that there were thousands. WyoHistory says over 1,000, with 800 mounted round the corral. Wikipedia puts both parties together at 300-1,000.
  • The soldiers' losses. Wikipedia gives 7 killed and 2 wounded; WyoHistory, from Hyde, 6 soldiers and 4 civilians killed. Gibson names the second private Doyle, not Boyle.
  • The company. WyoHistory calls it the 26th Infantry; most sources, and the game, the 27th.
  • The rifles. WyoHistory says a contractor brought about 700 rifles shortly before. The Army Heritage Museum says the 27th at the fort had received 195 by May 1867. Wikipedia adds some Henry rifles, and Spencers among the civilians.
  • The times. Gibson has about 07:00; Wikipedia, 07:30 to 13:30. The game starts the corral fight at about 09:15.
  • The order of the attacks. WyoHistory puts the big mounted charge last, around noon. Wikipedia has the mounted charge first and a final one from the south-east.
  • The site. Gibson's site, supported by cartridges found in 1916, is the one historians now accept.

The boy who found the corral

Sam Gibson was 18 on the day of the fight, the youngest soldier in the corral. In 1908 he came back and showed Charles Bezold where it had stood, by a fence along the Little Piney. Days later Bezold found cartridge cases and a crushed canteen there. Another survivor, Max Littmann, was taken in 1916 to a different spot, marked with a pipe. Grace Raymond Hebard of the University of Wyoming searched both. At Gibson's spot she found cartridges that fitted the Springfields and a piece of an oak wagon box; at the pipe, nothing. In 1919 Gibson marked the place again with a spike and a broomstick. The state put a granite stone there in 1921.

A worked example: the company

The Rules follow one medieval retinue. This chapter follows a company of British foot at Albuera on 16 May 1811, in Colborne's brigade, through the morning the Polish lancers came out of the hail. It uses the same rules and the Black-powder guns module, and, where dice are rolled, the dice given. The team builder made the company.

The company

The team builder rolls a company of foot of the Peninsular army. John Gallagher leads it: 3 terms, so he is 29, with Command 45. Its sergeant is Edmund Ross. Its best shot is Richard Costello, who fires his musket at 67% but defends at only 27%, with Bayonet 52. Its surgeon's mate is Benjamin Morris, Leechcraft 25. 16 men of the line follow them. They wear no armour.

On the field map

The company: out of the hail

The company stands in Colborne's brigade, in line, firing into the flank of Girard's column. The field opens overcast. When the lancers come, the field's own phase makes the weather a storm (six exchanges after the brigade first fires: no source gives the time), as the accounts tell it: a squall of rain and hail from the north. No one can see to aim past 109 yards (100 m), and each flintlock that fires misfires 45% of the time (30% in plain rain), as in Misfires.

The Polish lancers and hussars come out of the hail round the brigade's open flank, and are on it before it can turn. A lance strikes from 2 hexes away, a bayonet from 1, so a man on foot must close with the horseman to reach him. When the battalions break, the rout and the pursuit run as in Morale and the rout.

In the roller

The heroes' wounds are rolled in full, as in the fight.

The company: the ball

Before the storm, a French voltigeur, a regular, fires at Richard at 50% and rolls 12: a margin of 38. Against a ball, a leg takes a margin of 30 or more to be serious, so this one is serious. Richard dodges at 27% and rolls 71: no.

The ball strikes his left thigh. It breaks the bone. It bleeds 3, pain 2, and the leg is hurt. The wound carries shock, so he makes a stop check: Nerve 36, less 2 steps of pain, gives 16. He rolls 40 and fails by 24: he can do nothing, stunned, for 2 rounds. At 3 Blood a round, his 17 Blood lasts 5 rounds.

The company: the surgeon's mate

The best Leechcraft in the company is Benjamin's, and the GM rules that he can reach Richard from behind the line in time. He binds the thigh at Leechcraft 25 and rolls 11: he binds it, taking the bleeding down 2 steps to 1, as in First aid. Richard's broken thigh keeps him out of the fight.

The company: the lance

Then the lancers. One rides at Edmund from behind as the line gives way. The lancer is a veteran: he thrusts at 60% and rolls 14, a margin of 46. A lance uses the ordinary bands, serious from 20, so this is serious. Edmund turns to parry at 27% and rolls 47: no.

The point goes into his upper back. It bleeds 1, pain 2, and his arm is hurt. It carries no shock, so there is no stop check, and he keeps his feet. But a musket takes both hands, and with an arm hurt he cannot fire it, as in Wounds, so he can only defend. Untreated, the wound would kill him in days: it is for the surgeon tonight, and then the camp, as in Recovery.

For the GM

At Albuera the company is a score of men in a brigade, and the field map decides what happens to the brigade: Oman says three of Colborne's four battalions were nearly destroyed within five minutes. Keep the roller for the heroes inside it: a ball in the thigh, a surgeon's mate who gets there in time, a sergeant who stays on his feet with a lance wound in his back.
